title: Curriculum Unavailable

jokes.text: Pierce claiming credit for the potluck idea when all he said was 'I'm hungry'
jokes.setup: Someone credits Pierce for coming up with the idea of potluck dinners to keep the group together.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's actual 'idea' was just saying 'I'm hungry' — taking credit for nothing.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce self-aggrandizement — he inflates doing nothing into an achievement. Solid character work but fairly standard for his archetype.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I came up with the idea of a blanket fort. It's genius.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's just a blanket over some chairs.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Exactly! You know what Henry Ford said? 'If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.' Well, I didn't ask anyone. I just made a fort.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'All Henry Ford said was, "I need a ride."'
jokes.setup: Pierce is called out for claiming credit for saying 'I'm hungry.'
jokes.punchline: He defends himself with a completely fabricated and absurd reframing of history — Henry Ford as a lazy guy who just wanted a ride.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Pierce material. The logic is airtight in its absurdity — he's not wrong that innovation sometimes starts with a vague need, which makes the reframe feel almost defensible before you clock how insane it is. Perfect economy (seven words), highly quotable, and could ONLY come from Pierce. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, this? This is a deconstructed tater tot casserole with a microwave reduction and a Funyun crust, finished with a drizzle of nacho cheese coulis.

jokes.text: Troy's dish: 'bagel bites in a deconstructed hot pocket reduction with a Doritos glaze'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if that's a casserole Troy brought.
jokes.punchline: Troy describes his junk-food mashup in the elevated, pretentious language of fine cuisine.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the collision of lowbrow ingredients with highbrow culinary vocabulary. 'Deconstructed hot pocket reduction' is the peak — it's the right amount of absurd escalation. Troy's sincere earnestness ('I just really want to make my food') adds a layer of pathos that makes it richer.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Y'all are disgusting. This is what happens when you don't have a black woman in the group.

jokes.text: Troy: 'I just really want to make my food, you know.'
jokes.setup: Troy has described his absurd junk food dish in gourmet terms.
jokes.punchline: He drops the pretension and earnestly admits he just wants to cook, treating Bagel Bites-in-Hot-Pocket as a genuine culinary passion.
jokes.explanation: The sincerity is the joke. Troy's complete earnestness about his junk food as 'his food' is very on-brand and lands as a soft character beat. Works best as a capper to joke #3.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I brought a store-bought pie and told everyone I made it.

jokes.text: 'Did anybody bring anything that isn't poison?'
jokes.setup: The group has assembled their potluck contributions, which are universally terrible.
jokes.punchline: Jeff cuts through the pleasantries by calling all the food poison.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflation — functional and in-character, but doesn't rise above a standard straight-man one-liner. Economy is its main virtue.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed's gonna bring something cool to dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: We received a report of an explosive device.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, that's just Abed. He brought something delicious.

jokes.text: Jeff's contribution to the potluck is a pack of Lifesavers.
jokes.setup: Everyone is asked what they brought to the potluck dinner.
jokes.punchline: Jeff, the slick lawyer who coasts on minimal effort, brought a single pack of Lifesavers — the laziest possible 'food' contribution.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character shorthand for Jeff — maximum social participation, minimum actual effort. The visual gag of revealing the candy works well. Very much a Jeff joke.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Alright, freeze! We got a call about suspicious activity.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Inspector Spacetime, reporting for duty.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Look, I don't know what you're talking about, but if you could just come with me—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The Dregs are here, aren't they? I can feel their temporal distortion.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, buddy. The... Dregs. They're everywhere. We're gonna need to take you down to the precinct—in the Dreamscape.

jokes.text: 'See? Cool. Abed brought delicious police.'
jokes.setup: Someone speculates Abed is out getting something really cool for dinner; Troy says 'See? Cool.'
jokes.punchline: Abed returns accompanied by police officers — 'delicious police' — subverting the expectation that 'cool' meant food.
jokes.explanation: Troy's innocent 'delicious police' — treating cops as a food delivery — is perfectly Troy: unaware, optimistic, surreal. The misdirect from 'cool thing' to 'police escort' lands fast and the callback to the 'cool' setup is clean. Very quotable in context.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm familiar with Inspector Spacetime. In fact, that's kind of why I became a cop. I figured if I couldn't make it in the Inspector Spacetime fandom, at least I could enforce the law. Turns out I'm not very good at either.

jokes.text: Officer explains he knows Inspector Spacetime and says he'd take a bullet for Abed at Comic-Con, but here it's trespassing.
jokes.setup: Abed is in full Inspector Spacetime character mode while being arrested.
jokes.punchline: The cop is a fan who would fully indulge this at Comic-Con but distinguishes the convention context from the real world with a deadpan 'here in the real world, trespassing is a crime.'
jokes.explanation: The joke of a cop being a convention nerd who draws a clear line between 'Comic-Con acceptable behavior' and 'real world' is funny and observationally sharp. The character is a one-off but they write him well — a recognizable type (the geek-cop). Works as social commentary on fan culture.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Insp—... Inspector... Sp—... Space... time.

jokes.text: Officer: 'You think a guy becomes a cop because his prom night was a dream?'
jokes.setup: The group assumes the cop is a standard authority figure.
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals a traumatic backstory as motivation for becoming a cop, delivered with complete flatness.
jokes.explanation: Dark and efficient — the prom night detail is specific enough to feel real and sad, landing as an unexpected depth beat in an otherwise comic scene. The deadpan delivery in context is perfect. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: That's a 1987 clay brick, hand-fired in a kiln in suburban Pennsylvania. The subtle discoloration on the eastern face suggests exposure to approximately 2,000 hours of direct sunlight. Its weight distribution indicates it was likely part of a load-bearing wall in a mid-range residential structure. The mortar residue suggests it was removed sometime between 2003 and 2005. I'd appraise it at roughly $3.50.

jokes.text: Officer gives an extended, expert appraisal of an antique fire brick he found being used as a door prop, citing pre-Civil War dating and collector value.
jokes.setup: Officer is wrapping up the interaction and notices a brick propping open the door.
jokes.punchline: He launches into a detailed Antiques Roadshow-level assessment, completely derailing the scene with niche expertise about a brick.
jokes.explanation: This is a great slow-burn absurdist moment. The cop pivots from authority figure to brick connoisseur with complete sincerity, which is the joke — an expert in an unexpected domain deployed in the wrong context. The specificity ('uneven orange hue,' 'embossment') makes it funnier. Builds nicely toward the Antiques Roadshow punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Well, I appraised bricks for three years before I became a cop.

jokes.text: 'I watch a lot of Antiques Roadshow.'
jokes.setup: The officer has just delivered a suspiciously expert appraisal of an antique brick.
jokes.punchline: He explains his brick knowledge with a sheepish, casual admission — the mundane explanation for surreal expertise.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to joke #11. The understatement is the gag — the cop deflating his own moment of absurd expertise with a completely mundane explanation. Economy is essentially perfect at three words.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Did you know that every 12 seconds, someone in America is robbed? Every 45 seconds, someone is assaulted. Every 2 minutes, someone is raped. And every 22 minutes, someone is murdered.

jokes.text: Officer: 'Anyway, walk to your cars in pairs tonight. Rape's up 8%.'
jokes.setup: The officer is wrapping up his extended antique brick detour and pivoting back to official police business.
jokes.punchline: He casually delivers a crime statistic as a parting pleasantry, the brutal normalcy of the statistic made jarring by its conversational delivery.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'nifty piece of Americana' to crime statistic is whiplash comedy. The specificity of '8%' makes it funnier — this cop has memorized the exact figure but deploys it like weather small talk. Dark and efficient. The casualness is what elevates it past a cheap shock joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Rich people! Rich people! Hello? Yes, I have a brick that's worth sixty dollars. No, I don't know why. Can you come get it? Hello?

jokes.text: Troy: '$60? Hello? Rich people, Troy's joining you. Yes, I'll hold.'
jokes.setup: The officer mentioned the antique brick could sell for $50-60.
jokes.punchline: Troy treats $60 as life-changing wealth and immediately announces he's joining 'rich people' — miming a phone call to them.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Troy moment — his complete earnestness about $60 as an entry point into wealth is both endearing and funny. The pantomimed phone call to 'rich people' is delightfully absurd and very quotable. High character integration — no other character delivers this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed has this thing where he references TV and movies constantly. He sees the world through pop culture.

dialogue.speaker: Psychiatrist
dialogue.line: I see. Can you give me an example?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, like, he'll compare something to Robin Williams. You know, how Robin Williams used to be funny and weird like Mork, but now he's just creepy weird?

jokes.text: Abed described as 'adorable weird, like Mork from Ork, but since we got expelled, he's been creepy weird, like present-day Robin Williams.'
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to explain Abed's behavioral shift to the psychiatrist.
jokes.punchline: She lands on 'present-day Robin Williams' as the exemplar of creepy weird — a sharp, uncomfortable celebrity dig that contextualizes Abed's condition darkly.
jokes.explanation: The comparison structure (adorable weird vs. creepy weird) is clean, and 'Mork from Ork' as the positive pole is a funny specific choice. 'Present-day Robin Williams' is a sharp celebrity joke that takes a real risk. It's slightly uncomfortable given Williams' later mental health struggles, which makes it both funnier and darker in retrospect — but at airtime it reads as pointed pop-culture commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: I don't deal in 'crazy,' I deal in health.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: So what crazy thing happened?

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi: 'So how long has Abed needed a crazy amount of help?' (immediately after saying 'I don't deal in crazy')
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi explicitly says 'I don't deal in crazy, I deal in health.'
jokes.punchline: She immediately contradicts herself by saying 'how long has Abed needed a crazy amount of help?' — using 'crazy' in the same breath.
jokes.explanation: A tight structural joke — the speed of the self-contradiction is what makes it work. It immediately undermines the therapist's credibility and sets up the audience to distrust her, which pays off later. The craft is in the callback being instantaneous.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been thinking about Michael Bay. The guy's a visionary. His use of explosions and slow-motion really speaks to the human condition.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And Transformers? Transformers is cinema. Pure cinema. The way those robots transform really makes you question what it means to be alive.

jokes.text: 'There may have been a ramp-up.' (beat, then cutaway to flashback)
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi asks if all the behavior started after the expulsion.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's diplomatic 'there may have been a ramp-up' is a massive understatement that cues the entire clip-show structure of the episode.
jokes.explanation: Elegant structural joke that serves double duty — it's funny as a loaded understatement AND it's the mechanism that launches the episode's clip-show format. 'There may have been a ramp-up' is the perfect non-answer. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Brett Ratner is a visionary. His work has redefined cinema. I mean that sincerely.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: *internally* Why am I like this? I can feel myself doing it and I can't stop.

jokes.text: Abed and Troy discussing 'renting Tower Heist' and praising Brett Ratner as 'the new Spielberg'
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy appear to be having a normal conversation — but in context this is a flashback or recalled story.
jokes.punchline: They sincerely praise Brett Ratner — widely considered a hack director — as 'a master at storytelling' and 'the new Spielberg,' which is played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Abed, whose entire character is built around sophisticated film knowledge, sincerely praising Brett Ratner signals his mental deterioration more effectively than any clinical description. The escalation from 'hilarious thrill ride' to 'master of storytelling' to 'the new Spielberg' in three beats is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're traveling through another dimension. A dimension not only of sight and sound, but of mind. A journey into a wondrous shadow land whose boundaries are that of imagination. That's the signpost up ahead—your next stop: the Twilight Zone.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pierce Hawthorne sat down to eat a sandwich. An ordinary sandwich on an ordinary day. But this sandwich would change everything.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He reached for the bread. Two slices of whole wheat. Then came the lettuce. Crisp. Verdant. A sandwich was being born.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Mayonnaise. The condiment of kings. Applied with the precision of a surgeon. Of a artist. Of a man on the edge.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And then, the turkey. Slice after slice. Each one a testament to his hunger. To his loneliness. To his very existence in this cold, uncaring universe.

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi storms out saying 'You're a bad person. You're a bad person.'
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy's Brett Ratner praise reaches the conclusion that he's 'the new Spielberg.'
jokes.punchline: The psychiatrist, supposedly there to evaluate Abed, cannot handle this and leaves in ethical distress.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of who is offended — a mental health professional breaking professional composure over a film opinion. The repetition of 'You're a bad person' is funny in its simplicity. The meta-commentary that calling Ratner the new Spielberg is a greater offense than mental illness is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pierce walked into the room oldly, his bones creaking with the weight of his many, many years on this earth.

jokes.text: Abed narrating Pierce eating a sandwich as if he's a dying old man in a novel
jokes.setup: Abed narrates Pierce eating: 'Time enough at last to eat a sandwich. Though even he knew that this sandwich was nearer his last sandwich than his first.'
jokes.punchline: Pierce tries to object ('Abed, I'm trying to eat') and Abed incorporates the objection into his narration: 'He said, oldly, his brittle bones straining to support the weight of his wrinkly skin.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best gags. 'He said, oldly' is a genuinely inspired comic construction — Abed inventing an adverb to describe Pierce's age. The narration absorbing Pierce's protest seamlessly ('Stop narrating me' → 'He shouted to no one') shows superb structural craftsmanship. It's also excellent character integration: Abed's detached observational mode + Pierce's existential fragility collide perfectly. 'Oldly' alone is quotable. Clears the 8.0 craft anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pierce thinks he's the protagonist of some existential novel, completely unaware he's actually trapped in a mediocre TV show with a laugh track.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I take it back. I don't want to be in your novel.' → Abed: 'Pierce Hawthorne had nearly lost his grip on reality. Lately, he'd begun to think he was in a novel.'
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to opt out of Abed's narration.
jokes.punchline: Abed incorporates Pierce's very attempt to exit the fiction as evidence of Pierce's fictional delusion — a perfect meta-loop.
jokes.explanation: This is the best comedic construction in the episode. Abed turning Pierce's real-world protest ('I don't want to be in your novel') into in-novel evidence of Pierce's delusion is a genuinely clever meta-loop — the character's attempt to escape fiction becomes the fiction's plot. It's also darkly resonant given the episode's climax about shared delusion. The structure is nearly perfect: setup (Pierce opts out), inversion (Abed re-incorporates), escalation (the 'thinking he was in a novel' line). Among the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, what are you doing in my bedroom at 6 in the morning with a camera?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your natural confusion and irritation—perfect. Keep going.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not acting. Get out of my room.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Even better. The denial of performance while performing. This is gold.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, I'm serious. Leave.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the thing though—you're always serious, which makes it funny. Don't you see? You're my muse.

jokes.text: Abed is filming Jeff in his bedroom at 4:30 AM saying 'Cut. We got it. One more for safety.'
jokes.setup: Jeff wakes to find Abed in his bedroom in the middle of the night with a camera.
jokes.punchline: Abed is unfazed, fully in director mode, calling 'cut' and requesting 'one more for safety' — treating Jeff's real life as a film set.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed-going-wrong behavior. The horror of being filmed in your bedroom is subverted by Abed's total nonchalance and his use of proper film set vocabulary. It's cringe-comedy that also advances the episode's thesis about Abed's deteriorating grip on reality-vs-fiction. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed is not crazy. He's just... creative. And okay, yes, sometimes he does things that are a little crazy-town banana pants, but that doesn't mean he's actually crazy!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'You mean committed to his character work, right? Because he already is. Abed, show him your Don Draper.' / Abed: 'Cigarettes.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi says she thinks Abed should be 'committed.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff misunderstands it as a compliment about dedication; when corrected, he pivots to having Abed demonstrate his Don Draper impression — which Abed delivers as a single word: 'Cigarettes.'
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke with great economy. The 'committed to his character work' misdirect is a clean setup, but 'Cigarettes' as the totality of an Abed-as-Don-Draper impression is the sharper punchline — it's a perfect distillation of the character's essence into one word. Very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We're all a little crazy. I mean, I take pills for my back pain, but that's just medicine.

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi: 'Talk to me about crazy-town banana pants.'
jokes.setup: Annie has just coined the phrase 'crazy-town banana pants.'
jokes.punchline: The psychiatrist, completely deadpan, adopts the absurd phrase as clinical terminology.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The doctor treating 'crazy-town banana pants' as a legitimate clinical topic worth pursuing is a great deadpan move. Economy is excellent — five words do everything.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You can borrow my coat, but you have to follow these rules.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No wearing it on Tuesdays.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You can't let it touch the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: If someone compliments it, you have to tell them it's mine.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And you absolutely cannot wear it in a school building, near a school building, or within a two-block radius of a school building.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Also, no sitting in it. Only standing or lying down.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Who among us hasn't had the odd banana in his or her pants, right?' / [pause] / 'I have.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to rhetorically defend the group as universally a bit crazy.
jokes.punchline: His rhetorical 'who among us' is followed by a pause and then his own literal self-incriminating answer.
jokes.explanation: Good callback extension. Jeff's rhetorical device collapses because he volunteers himself — and the literal interpretation of 'banana in pants' makes it funnier. The pause before 'I have' is essential timing.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Troy! You cannot bring that in here!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But Shirley, it says right here on the box: 'all-terrain vehicle.' All terrain means all terrain!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That does not mean inside the apartment!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well technically, this is terrain. I'm standing on it right now.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'How long does peyote last? Just asking for a friend.'
jokes.setup: The group is sharing stories about their crazy Greendale experiences.
jokes.punchline: 'Just asking for a friend' — the transparent deflection is funny because it's Shirley, the most outwardly religious/proper member of the group, casually asking about drug duration.
jokes.explanation: 'Just asking for a friend' is a tired phrase, but on Shirley it lands because of character contrast. Her prim religiosity makes the drug question funnier. The joke trades almost entirely on character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm giving away all my possessions because I came in second place in the dreamers competition.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Second place makes me unstoppable!

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's morning show 'Troy and Abed and Annie in the Morning' — the jingle playing in the apartment at an inappropriate time.
jokes.setup: Annie confronts Troy and Abed about the cameras in the apartment.
jokes.punchline: The 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' jingle plays — but adapted to include Annie — revealing they've started a show without telling her.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag extension. The 'and Annie' addition is a simple but effective joke — they've colonized her apartment and incorporated her into their world without asking. Fans of the show will appreciate the callback to the season-long morning show gag.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Little misadventures? We're men! We go on adventures. Big, manly adventures.

jokes.text: Jeff gives Annie his coat, then immediately itemizes all the restrictions: no eating, drinking, sweating, bending at elbows, no chairs with backrests, wooden hangers only.
jokes.setup: Jeff generously gives Annie his coat when she seems cold.
jokes.punchline: The gesture is immediately revealed as not generous at all — he's essentially lending her a museum piece with a 20-point terms-of-service agreement.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating character joke. Jeff's vanity about his wardrobe is well-established, and the specificity of 'wooden hangers only' and 'no bending at the elbows' escalates nicely. The generous gesture collapsing under the weight of his narcissism is a perfect Jeff beat.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you want to commit Abed to an institution?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'd like to work in a place where people respect the work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed, that's not what committed means!

jokes.text: Pierce reacts to Troy's all-terrain wheelchair with 'Yes, I can. It's all-terrain, dummy.'
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Pierce) tries to tell Troy he can't bring the wheelchair in somewhere.
jokes.punchline: Troy defends it on the grounds that it's 'all-terrain' — the technical spec is treated as a universal pass.
jokes.explanation: Decent topper. 'All-terrain, dummy' is a funny defense that treats product specs as legal protection. Mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: I mean a mental institution.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, that's what I said — marriage!

jokes.text: Shirley gives each group member something from her kids — karate championship second place trophy for Pierce — 'Now I'll be unstoppable!'
jokes.setup: Shirley gives Pierce her son's second-place karate trophy as a gift.
jokes.punchline: Pierce receives a child's second-place trophy with delirious excitement: 'Now I'll be unstoppable!'
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce character beat. His inflated self-image meeting a child's second-place trophy is a perfect size mismatch. 'Now I'll be unstoppable!' is funny precisely because his enthusiasm is completely unironic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, can we please get some comic relief here? This is getting dark.

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi squeezes the stress ball after being told not to — 'I'm sorry.' / Jeff/Annie: 'Uh-huh.'
jokes.setup: The group has just finished telling the psychiatrist about an intimate group object (the stress ball).
jokes.punchline: She grabs it and squeezes it anyway — an authority figure behaving like a child, then offering a transparently insincere apology.
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe beat. The psychiatrist violating the group's space is a small power inversion, but the joke is fairly light. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Please, you have to believe me. Abed isn't crazy, he just processes the world differently!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A mental institution is not a... a crazy people jail. It's a facility for psychiatric care and treatment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm speaking with the utmost formality and gravity here.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Take that back. Our adventures are very manly.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi dismisses the group's shared experiences as 'little misadventures.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's wounded defense insists on the manliness of their community college adventures.
jokes.explanation: Light character beat. Jeff's ego being pricked by 'misadventures' is consistent, but the joke doesn't have a very sharp punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Abed is like a snowflake - unique and beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Or he's cold, isolated, and will eventually melt into nothing, which is basically what happens to all of us.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'You mean like marriage?' / Dr. Heidi: 'I mean a mental institution.' / Jeff: 'Ah. So do I.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi says she means 'an institution' (mental institution). Jeff plays through two wrong interpretations — marriage, then corrects himself.
jokes.punchline: 'Ah. So do I' — Jeff claims he knew all along, as if 'mental institution' was his joke about marriage.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom wordplay on 'institution.' The 'Ah. So do I' recovery is what elevates it above a standard double-meaning joke — Jeff's confidence in claiming the joke retroactively is very in-character. The final 'Will someone please help me lighten the mood?' from an unnamed character is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We survived Greendale. We have the scars to prove it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We had lockers.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. Lockers.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Ah. So do I.' (after Dr. Heidi says she means a mental institution)
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi corrects that she means a mental institution, not marriage.
jokes.punchline: Abed agrees he also means a mental institution — revealing he's been aware of the gravity of his situation the entire time, or possibly agreeing ironically.
jokes.explanation: Very economical Abed joke. His deadpan agreement has perfect ambiguity — is he being literal, self-aware, or making a dark joke about his own situation? Three words that do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Attention students, I have an important announcement about the upcoming midterm examination.

jokes.text: Unknown character: 'Will someone please help me lighten the mood?'
jokes.setup: Jeff's marriage/institution joke attempt ends awkwardly.
jokes.punchline: Someone asks for help lightening the mood after Jeff's joke was supposed to have done exactly that.
jokes.explanation: Functional button joke, but weak character integration (unclear who delivers it) and the idea of someone asking for help lightening the mood after a failed joke attempt is a fairly standard beat. Serviceable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Knight to E4.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Neigh!

jokes.text: Troy: 'Please, Mr. Dr. psychiatrist, sir, please don't send my best friend to crazy people jail.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi recommends committing Abed to a mental institution.
jokes.punchline: Troy's earnest, overly formal pleading — 'Mr. Dr. psychiatrist, sir' — combined with 'crazy people jail' (his term for a mental institution) reveals both his care for Abed and his limited vocabulary for clinical settings.
jokes.explanation: 'Crazy people jail' is a perfect Troy coinage — it's exactly what a kind, earnest, not-particularly-worldly person would call a psychiatric institution. 'Mr. Dr. psychiatrist, sir' shows Troy's attempt to be maximally respectful with uncertain vocabulary. Very high character integration: this is irreducibly Troy. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Can I get a blowjob shot?

dialogue.speaker: Cafeteria Worker
dialogue.line: No. And stop trying to make that a thing.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'like a snowflake who gets bent out of shape when you mix up Star Wars and Space Treks' / Britta: 'Or a serial killer's signature.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to convince the doctor that Abed is merely unique, not dangerous.
jokes.punchline: Jeff uses an Abed-specific analogy (mixing up Trek/Wars franchises sends him into distress). Britta contributes 'or a serial killer's signature' — adding an example that completely undercuts Jeff's argument.
jokes.explanation: The 'Space Treks' detail is a funny Abed-specific character detail. Britta's 'serial killer's signature' is the sharper joke — she's trying to help but inadvertently comparing Abed's uniqueness to a homicidal pattern. Classic Britta: well-intentioned, poorly executed. Good character comedy for both.

jokes.text: Professor in flashback: 'My name is Pwofussa Wobinswin. Who's weady to weawn?'
jokes.setup: The group shares memories of Greendale being a 'messed-up place.'
jokes.punchline: A professor with a severe speech impediment addresses the class — played completely straight as a Greendale faculty member.
jokes.explanation: Speech impediment humor is a lazy comedy shortcut (hence the low 'earned vs. cheap' score). It gets some lift from the Greendale-absurdism context — the idea that this person somehow became a professor — but it doesn't transcend the cheap laugh mechanism.

jokes.text: Dean's parking solution for the job fair: a chess-like system using students as pieces in an outdoor lot
jokes.setup: Britta objects to the Dean's parking solution as 'inhumane.'
jokes.punchline: The Dean's system appears to involve students positioned as chess pieces. 'Vicki to Queen 3. Neigh.' — suggesting the system is live chess with actual people, some assigned horse roles.
jokes.explanation: 'Neigh' — a student assigned the role of a chess horse making horse sounds — is a lovely absurdist detail. The Dean using human chess for parking management is perfectly in his wheelhouse of insane, spectacle-based institutional decisions. The 'Vicki to Queen 3' precision suggests he takes this very seriously, which is funnier than if it were played as chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: How are you doing today, Pierce?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I'll tell you, Doc. Every time I close my eyes, I see faces. Angry faces. And they're all screaming my name. But not in a good way, you know? More like a 'we're gonna get you' way.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, it's sundowning time.

jokes.text: Chess game visual: 'Vicki to Queen 3.' / 'Neigh.' — a horse sound used as a chess move announcement.
jokes.setup: A chess game is happening in what appears to be a Greendale classroom.
jokes.punchline: 'Neigh' — someone announces a knight's move by making the sound of a horse, treating chess notation as requiring animal sounds.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever absurdist gag. 'Neigh' as a knight move announcement is an inspired tiny joke — the internal logic (the knight is a horse) is correct but the execution is surreal. Perfect economy: one word does all the work. Rewatch bonus for catching it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone, I need you to exit the building in a prompt yet orderly fashion with the utmost urgency while maintaining a positive attitude and perhaps even smiling as we vacate these premises immediately!

jokes.text: Professor: 'There's one every year. I will not tolerate clowning.'
jokes.setup: A student has been ejected for apparently saying 'fries.'
jokes.punchline: The professor gravely treats answering 'fries' as 'clowning' — a word far too serious for the offense.
jokes.explanation: Button to joke #30. The gap between the apparent offense and the gravity of 'I will not tolerate clowning' is the joke. Works as a brief escalation cap.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone, we need to evacuate immediately! This is a fire emergency!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And I just want you all to know... before we potentially never see each other again... you've meant so much to me. Each and every one of you.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff, your confidence and leadership... Britta, your passion... Troy, your innocence... Abed, your uniqueness... Annie, your dedication... Shirley, your warmth... Pierce, your... presence.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And I hope that if we survive this, you'll remember that your dean cares about you!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Now GO! Before the fire consumes us all! And please think of me fondly!

jokes.text: Student tries to get past a man blocking the hallway who is talking about 'a long road tomorrow'
jokes.setup: A student simply needs to get past someone in a hallway.
jokes.punchline: The man blocking the way addresses them as 'Rufus' and says 'Slow your bones... we got a long road tomorrow' — a completely disconnected, apparently in-character bit that makes no logical sense in the hallway context.
jokes.explanation: One of the 'Greendale is a weird place' vignette jokes. The confusion of registers (normal hallway encounter vs. cryptic wagon-trail delivery) is funny but the joke is underdeveloped and doesn't quite land without the visual context.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm here to check on you. How are you feeling?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You need to leave. Get out of here.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I said get out! Out! OUT!

jokes.text: The 'Welcome... to ladders.' class reveal
jokes.setup: The scene builds up with 'Welcome...' — implying something grand or academic is about to be announced.
jokes.punchline: '...to ladders.' A class dedicated to ladders, delivered with apparent sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical absurdist joke. The deliberate dramatic pause ('Welcome...') creates expectation, 'to ladders.' destroys it. The two-word punchline is essentially perfect — any additional explanation would ruin it. This is exactly the kind of joke Community does best: it simultaneously satirizes community college course offerings and delivers pure comic absurdism. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Pizza day has been cancelled due to... unforeseen circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: But Dean, we were looking forward to it!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I know, I know. It's just that I've decided to implement a new policy: pizza is now reserved exclusively for my most... academically promising students.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: That's not fair!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Life isn't fair. But my office is very fair. And very well-stocked with pepperoni.

jokes.text: Reaction beat: two students share a knowing look after 'Welcome to ladders.'
jokes.setup: 'Welcome to ladders.' is announced.
jokes.punchline: Two students exchange a look that says 'just checking' — they compare reactions to validate the absurdity they're both experiencing.
jokes.explanation: Brief visual beat — 'just wanted to see if we got the same thing' — that serves as a button to the ladders joke. Functional, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You are the best study group, the best study group in the whole world. You're so special, so special, Jeffrey loves you so much. Jeffrey loves you, Jeffrey loves you, Jeffrey loves you so much.

jokes.text: Pierce says he was at Greendale 'longer than anybody' and he's 'fine' — group's dubious reaction.
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to rebut concerns about Greendale's negative effects by citing himself as a fine example.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Heidi asks 'How are you?' Pierce's response — '3:30. Uh-oh.' — reveals he's immediately confused time.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce character joke. His confident self-assessment ('I'm fine') is immediately demolished by his apparent sundowning — answering 'How are you?' with the time. The term 'sundowning' (dementia symptom where confusion worsens in the afternoon) is used by another character, adding a dark specificity. Great economy in the collapse.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Paintball is important to me because it's the only time this show becomes interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Also, it's basically just an excuse for the writers to do a action movie parody while ignoring character development for 40 minutes.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I was there longer than anybody, and I'm fine.' / Dr. Heidi: 'How are you?' / Pierce: 'Why do you ask? 3:30.'
jokes.setup: Pierce insists Greendale wasn't bad and that he's fine as evidence.
jokes.punchline: The doctor asks 'how are you?' as a clinical probe. Pierce's response — 'Why do you ask? 3:30.' — is a non-sequitur that suggests cognitive disorientation. 'Sundowning' is then referenced.
jokes.explanation: Dark joke that earns it. 'Sundowning' (a symptom of dementia that worsens in the late afternoon) is a clinical term the show deploys with precision — Pierce claiming to be fine while literally sundowning is sad and funny simultaneously. '3:30' as his disoriented response is both specific and haunting. This is Community doing dark character comedy responsibly.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The prize is two tickets to see the community theater production of 'Cats' featuring special guest appearances by... well, let's just say some very famous people from the '70s.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Pass.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: Hard pass.

dialogue.speaker: Troy Barnes
dialogue.line: No thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Abed Nadir
dialogue.line: I'd rather watch the actual cats.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton bursting in to warn the group about a fire — but he wanted to tell THEM first before general evacuation because he doesn't know what he'd do without them
jokes.setup: Dean appears and seems to be delivering urgent fire-safety news.
jokes.punchline: He pauses to have a sentimental moment with the study group DURING AN ACTUAL FIRE, saying 'I know it's not right to play favorites, but...' — the life-threatening situation is secondary to his feelings.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton character comedy. His obsession with the study group overrides his institutional responsibility even during a fire emergency — the gap between the stakes and his behavior is enormous and very funny. 'I know it's not right to play favorites, but it is no more right to sit on your feelings' during a building fire is exactly the Dean's character distilled. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Community college isn't some magical place where—

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Jeff, you've fought a paintball war, joined a cult, and your study group has stopped an actual conspiracy. You once had to negotiate with a dementia patient who thought she was a secret agent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Okay, but that's just—

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: You're not delusional about community college being mundane. You're delusional if you think any of that was normal.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Darcy, you've got a cold. You're sick. Go home! Get out of here!'
jokes.setup: During the fire evacuation chaos, Jeff encounters a student named Darcy.
jokes.punchline: Jeff uses the fire chaos as cover to dismiss someone from their presence by dramatically (and falsely) declaring them sick — an absurd non-sequitur in the middle of an evacuation.
jokes.explanation: Decent throwaway gag — Jeff using authority-theater to dismiss someone during a crisis is in-character, but the joke is thin without more context for who Darcy is or why Jeff would care.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've accomplished more than most men. I've built a business empire, I've won awards, I've been recognized by my peers.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've dined with senators, I've golfed with CEOs, I've— I once made eye contact with Clint Eastwood at an airport.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: He nodded at me. A full nod. Not just a glance—a nod.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe we got here too late for pizza. Worst pizza day ever. Oh, darn it. What am I gonna do with all this garbage?'
jokes.setup: A fire is happening at the school.
jokes.punchline: Someone's primary concern is missing pizza day and disposing of garbage — during a building fire. The gap between the emergency and the mundane complaint is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Background gag that works via misplaced priorities — the fire is irrelevant, what matters is pizza. Thin character integration but the mundane-vs.-emergency contrast is a reliable structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: We need to confiscate his pens.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Isn't that a bit extreme?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: It's not confiscation, it's a psychological experiment. We're studying the effects of pen deprivation on patient behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: You're just calling it an experiment so it sounds scientific.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's what makes me a doctor.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton secretly pulls six pieces of pizza for the study group during a fire evacuation
jokes.setup: Everyone lamented getting there too late for pizza.
jokes.punchline: The Dean, mid-evacuation, took time to save pizza specifically for the study group — 'Psst, it's me, the Dean. I pulled the last six pieces of pizza for you.'
jokes.explanation: Beautiful Dean moment — his favoritism toward the study group extends to pizza triage during an emergency. Ties together his 'I don't know what I'd do without you' speech and the pizza complaint. The 'Psst, it's me, the Dean' whisper suggests he understands this is not normal behavior even as he does it. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Mi hambre es... bombero... suspensores.

jokes.text: Dean: 'We have a few students with birthdays today, but, hey, why single them out? What about the students who aren't celebrating anything at all? Are they any less special?'
jokes.setup: A routine birthday announcement at Greendale.
jokes.punchline: The Dean subverts the birthday recognition to offer equal consolation prizes to non-birthday students — his pathological need to avoid exclusion collides with common sense.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp Dean character comedy. His institutional announcements always reveal a crippling anxiety about exclusion and special treatment (unless it's the study group). The logic is internally consistent — if birthday students are special, surely ALL students are equally special — delivered with the earnestness of a true believer.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Shared psychosis is a rare psychiatric syndrome where delusional beliefs are transmitted from one individual to another.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: It's much like how the swing dance revival of the 1990s spread through social groups with no rational basis whatsoever.

jokes.text: Dean's personalized 'Happy Birthday' song naming every study group member — including 'Jeffrey' twice and messing up the meter
jokes.setup: The Dean has just questioned why birthday students should be singled out.
jokes.punchline: He then immediately sings a song that names the study group members specifically — including 'Jeffrey' twice — proving his stated egalitarianism is just a front for more study group favoritism.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic callback to joke #40 — the Dean's 'egalitarian' speech about not singling out birthday students immediately becomes a personalized anthem for his favorite people. Naming 'Jeffrey' twice suggests he lost himself thinking about Jeff mid-song. The song lyrics ('just a few of the most special students in the world') perfectly contradict his universalist framing. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Because I'm not who you think I am!

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: I'm actually a deep-cover operative for the Belgian government, and I've been using Greendale as a front to smuggle artisanal waffles into the country!

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Everything you know is a lie. My name isn't even Heidi. It's... Brunhilde.

jokes.text: Paintball scene: Dean saves Abed, then gives him prize tickets to see 'Chicago' at Greendale Civic Center with George Wendt and Stefanie Powers
jokes.setup: Dean dramatically saves Abed in a paintball battle and offers him prize tickets to 'Chicago.'
jokes.punchline: The celebrity lineup — George Wendt (Norm from Cheers, a minor TV celebrity) and Stefanie Powers (Hart to Hart, a dated TV actress) — is pathetically un-special, confirmed by the audience reaction: 'Lame!'
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the gap between the drama of the paintball rescue and the deflation of the prize. The deliberate pauses after 'Chicago' and 'George Wendt and...' (beat) '...Stefanie Powers' suggest even the Dean knows it's underwhelming. 'Lame!' being the natural reaction is the perfect button. Good escalation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: So what brings you in today?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not feeling well.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Hmm, yes. Well, as a Persian doctor, I can tell you...

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm actually half-Iraqi, half-Polish.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Heidi
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, I should probably tell you I'm not actually a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm not actually sick. I just wanted to see if you'd figure it out.

jokes.text: Abed: 'It just feels forced.' (about paintball)
jokes.setup: The Dean tells Abed paintball is important and he wanted him to win.
jokes.punchline: Abed says it 'just feels forced' — a meta-commentary on the show's repeated paintball episodes, delivered in-character by the most meta character on the show.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant meta-joke. By Season 3, the paintball episodes have become a beloved Community tradition — and Abed, the show's most self-aware character, breaking from his Inspector Spacetime mode to call paintball 'forced' is perfect meta-commentary on the show's own recurring gimmick. It's also genuinely funny because it's true — by Season 3, fans had a complicated relationship with paintball returns. Only Abed could deliver this. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: Group realizes all their positive Greendale memories feature Dean Pelton.
jokes.setup: Jeff notes that all the great Greendale memories they've shared have something in common.
jokes.punchline: 'I was barely in them?' — the Dean ironically suggests the wrong answer, before Jeff says it's actually that they all feature the Dean.
jokes.explanation: The Dean's self-deprecating wrong answer ('I was barely in them?') is funny because we've just seen him dominate all the flashbacks. The punchline being that he IS central to all of them doubles as genuine character work — the Dean's care for the study group has been constant even when he seems peripheral.

dialogue.speaker: Assistant
dialogue.line: So what's the next phase of your plan?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, I'm gonna be honest with you. I'm kind of making this up as I go.

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi's 'psychosis reveal': claims Greendale doesn't exist and the group are mental patients who shared a delusion.
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi has been listening to the group's Greendale memories.
jokes.punchline: She claims the memories are a 'shared psychosis' — that Greendale was a mental institution, not a community college, and they were patients together. This is a meta joke about sitcoms: the events of Community ARE absurd enough to be a mass delusion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's high-concept jokes. The 'Greendale doesn't exist / you're mental patients' reveal is a brilliant meta move — it acknowledges that the show's events (paintball wars, alternate timelines, zombie outbreaks) are so absurd they could genuinely be symptoms of psychosis. The joke works both as an in-universe twist AND as meta-commentary on the show's own absurdity. This is Community doing what it does best: weaponizing genre awareness for comedy. High originality because few sitcoms would construct an entire episode around questioning their own premise.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Welcome back to Subway, where we serve sandwiches and loneliness.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're taking calls tonight from people who have nowhere else to be.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: First caller, you're on the air. Tell us about your evening.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And please, make it sadder than our sandwiches.

jokes.text: 'This fantastical community college where everything that happens is unbelievably ridiculous and it all revolves around you as a group.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi is making the case that Greendale is too absurd to be real.
jokes.punchline: She's describing the actual Community premise — a 'fantastical community college where everything is unbelievably ridiculous' — directly to the characters who live it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta joke. The psychiatrist articulates the show's own premise as evidence of psychosis — 'everything that happens is unbelievably ridiculous and it all revolves around you as a group' is an accurate description of Community as a television show. This kind of self-awareness is Community at its peak. The joke works because it's not just self-referential — it's self-critical in a playful way.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And that's our show. But before you go to bed tonight, I want you to think about the difference between fun scary and real-life scary. Fun scary is like, a nightmare where you're being chased by a clown. Real-life scary is like, a nightmare where you're not being chased by a clown, but you're still worried about your student loans.

jokes.text: Secret trampoline scene: students discover a hidden trampoline, exchange delighted looks
jokes.setup: The psychiatrist is trying to convince the group that Greendale was a shared psychosis because it was 'unbelievably ridiculous.'
jokes.punchline: Cut to: students discovering a secret trampoline, jumping with glee — a visual confirmation that yes, Greendale really was that ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Perfect show-don't-tell comedic juxtaposition. The psychiatrist's claim that Greendale was too absurd to be real is immediately illustrated by a secret campus trampoline being joyfully discovered — which somehow makes both points (Greendale IS ridiculous AND that's why they loved it). Brilliant structural placement.

jokes.text: Full-group paintball charge scene with 'For Greendale! Charge!' and Leonard being injured
jokes.setup: An inspirational call to arms — 'For Greendale! Charge!'
jokes.punchline: Leonard, the elderly background character, is immediately taken out with 'Yow!'/'Ooh!' — the heroic charge has an immediate first casualty.
jokes.explanation: Leonard getting taken out is a reliable recurring gag. The 'For Greendale' sincerity punctured by an immediate casualty is a classic war-film parody beat. Functional but not inventive.

jokes.text: Baby Boomer Santa song in a holiday flashback
jokes.setup: A holiday memory from Greendale is recalled.
jokes.punchline: 'Baby Boomer Santa / Thank you for everything / You're welcome, you're welcome / For everything in the world' — a holiday song about Santa as a baby boomer that makes no sense but sounds sincere.
jokes.explanation: Absurdist song joke that works because it's delivered with complete sincerity. 'Baby Boomer Santa' as a concept is funny — the generational specificity is unexpected. The call-and-response structure ('You're welcome, you're welcome') adds to the absurdity. Terry's interruption adds another layer.

jokes.text: Memory-within-a-memory: 'Remember when we went camping? Yes. Remember when we painted the nursery? Yes. Remember when we remembered going camping while we were in the nursery?'
jokes.setup: Group members are sharing nostalgic memories at a party.
jokes.punchline: The memories escalate to 'Remember when we remembered going camping while we were in the nursery?' — a memory of a memory, which is an impossible recursive construction.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever structural joke. The escalation from normal nostalgic beats to a 'memory of a memory' is an absurdist logical loop that also meta-comments on how clip shows create nested nostalgia (nostalgia about nostalgia). The structure perfectly mirrors the episode's clip-show conceit. Original and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Pierce's delusional boast: 'I'm a millionaire, I'm an inventor, I'm a legend, and I had sex with Eartha Kitt.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is in a flashback, apparently in a deteriorating mental state.
jokes.punchline: His list of self-aggrandizing claims escalates from plausible (millionaire) to improbable (inventor, legend) to bizarre (sex with Eartha Kitt) — delivered as though the last item is the crown jewel.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's escalating ego combined with an unexpected specific celebrity name is very strong. 'Eartha Kitt' is exactly right — an actress/singer of a certain vintage, slightly obscure to modern audiences, but perfect for Pierce's generational frame of reference. The rhythm of the four-item list (millionaire → inventor → legend → Eartha Kitt) escalates perfectly. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Nurse's reaction to Pierce: 'It's sad. Should we increase their lithium?' / Other nurse: 'Not yet. I want to see what happens if we confiscate one of their pens.'
jokes.setup: Staff watch the group's delusions play out during the holiday party flashback.
jokes.punchline: The nurse's desire to run an informal experiment by confiscating a pen reveals that the psychiatric staff are treating these patients as subjects of casual curiosity rather than care.
jokes.explanation: Smart dark joke that retroactively seeds doubt about whether this 'memory' is real or planted (by the fake psychiatrist's false narrative). 'What happens if we confiscate one of their pens' as casual experimentation is both darkly funny and structurally important — it foreshadows the reveal. The nonchalance is key.

jokes.text: Spanish competency challenge: 'Mi hambre es bombero tirantes.' (translated roughly as 'My hunger is a fireman suspenders')
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi challenges the group: if Greendale is real, do any of them speak Spanish after three years of Spanish study group?
jokes.punchline: The only Spanish offered is a meaningless word-salad sentence — proving they learned nothing, delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke that also works as series-long meta-commentary — the Spanish study group has never demonstrably learned any Spanish in three seasons. The specific sentence chosen is funny because it sounds just plausible enough that someone might think it's real before it falls apart. Great economy and earned by seasons of setup.

jokes.text: Dr. Heidi: '...like that time all those people got into swing dance music back in the '90s.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Heidi is explaining how shared delusions can spread through groups.
jokes.punchline: She compares the group's shared Greendale psychosis to the '90s swing dance revival — an extremely specific, slightly embarrassing cultural moment that is a funny choice for 'mass delusion.'
jokes.explanation: Good specific pop-culture reference as analogy. The '90s swing dance revival is an inspired choice — specific enough to be funny, accurate enough to resonate, embarrassing enough to sting. Strengthens the therapist's argument comedically even as the plot is about to undermine her.

jokes.text: Psychiatrist is exposed as a fraud — mid-phone call: 'Yeah, it's me. No, I think they bought it. I had to do a little riffing at the end, but I was pretty convincing.'
jokes.setup: The whole therapy session has been presented as legitimate.
jokes.punchline: The psychiatrist is caught on a phone call admitting she's a fake who improvised ('riffing at the end') her way through the session — the expert was making it up.
jokes.explanation: Solid plot-twist joke. 'I had to do a little riffing at the end' retroactively makes all her previous confident diagnoses funnier and contextualizes the swing-dance comparison as desperate improvisation. The reveal also validates all the hints (her instant self-contradiction with 'crazy') placed earlier.

jokes.text: Fake psychiatrist: 'Well, if it looks like I'm sneaking out the window, it's just a symptom of your deepening psychosis.'
jokes.setup: Caught as a fake, the psychiatrist is physically trying to escape.
jokes.punchline: She attempts to gaslight her way out — attributing her visible escape attempt to the group's mental illness rather than her own guilt.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke structure — she weaponizes the very therapy framework she was using to gaslight them, applying 'deepening psychosis' to cover her literal escape. It's also meta-commentary on gaslighting as a structure. 'If it looks like I'm sneaking out the window' is very quotable and the logic is brilliantly circular. Clears the 7.5-8 craft threshold.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm literally carrying a Greendale backpack. I have, like, 1,000 pictures of the campus on my phone. I have children I see every day.'
jokes.setup: The fake psychiatrist tries to maintain that Greendale doesn't exist.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's evidence for Greendale's existence escalates from physical objects to photos to — most entertainingly — 'I have children I see every day,' which is a hilarious way to describe being a teacher.
jokes.explanation: 'I have children I see every day' as Jeff's way of describing his students is both funny (the depersonalized description) and character-revealing (he doesn't think of himself as particularly invested in them). Good escalation in the list structure.

jokes.text: Fake psychiatrist: 'Because, Ms. Edison, Greendale is purgatory, and I am the devil.'
jokes.setup: The group demands to know why she lied to make them think they were crazy.
jokes.punchline: She offers 'Greendale is purgatory and I am the devil' — a dramatic, ridiculous overclaim that is clearly a stall tactic.
jokes.explanation: Funny stall-tactic villain overclaim. The gap between 'fake psychiatrist hired for a scheme' and 'I am the devil' is funny — she's reaching for maximum threat and landing on nonsense. Jeff's 'Stop letting him make you realize stuff' response is a good button.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Stop letting him make you realize stuff.'
jokes.setup: The group starts buying into the fake psychiatrist's dramatic 'I am the devil' claim.
jokes.punchline: Jeff cuts off the moment with a pure anti-therapy sentiment: don't let the bad guy do therapy on us.
jokes.explanation: Very Jeff — he's simultaneously aware that the moment is manipulative AND trying to prevent his friends from having a genuine emotional realization, which is his standard defensive mode. 'Stop letting him make you realize stuff' is quotable and sharp. The 'him' despite the psychiatrist being a woman is either a character error or a deliberate odd choice.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'He's Arabic.' / Another: 'Also Polish.' / Fake doc: 'Whatever. I'm a fake psychiatrist, not a fake ethnologist.'
jokes.setup: The fake psychiatrist refers to Abed as 'the Indian kid.'
jokes.punchline: The group corrects her ('He's Arabic. Also Polish.'), and her retort — 'I'm a fake psychiatrist, not a fake ethnologist' — is a perfect deflection that also admits her fraud in a casually devastating way.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I'm a fake psychiatrist, not a fake ethnologist' is structurally perfect — it uses the character's newly-admitted fraud as the basis of her defense, which is an elegant loop. The 'whatever' dismissal followed by an oddly precise claim (I fake THIS, not THAT) suggests a professional pride in the specific nature of her fakery. Very quotable. Close to the 8.0 craft anchor in elegance and economy.

jokes.text: Chang 'predicting future crimes' by sitting in an empty room, apparently waiting for crimes to happen
jokes.setup: The group remembers why they suspected something was wrong with Greendale — Chang was acting strangely.
jokes.punchline: Chang is sitting alone claiming to be 'predicting future crimes,' apparently a self-appointed pre-crime unit of one.
jokes.explanation: Chang as a self-appointed Minority Report pre-cog is excellently absurd. The image of him sitting alone in an empty room waiting to predict crimes is a strong visual gag (inferred). 'Now I'm sick' and 'You are a pre-cog!' are good escalating beats.

jokes.text: Troy: 'You are a pre-cog!'
jokes.setup: Chang claims to be predicting future crimes; someone says 'now I'm sick' (fulfilling Chang's 'prediction').
jokes.punchline: Troy is completely sincerely impressed, treating Chang's 'prediction' as genuine precognition.
jokes.explanation: Troy's genuine amazement at a coincidence is very on-brand. The Minority Report reference ('pre-cog') works for a character who thinks in pop-culture terms. Good character integration but not a structurally complex joke.

jokes.text: Britta: 'He's out there somewhere, alone and cold and most likely trying to cobble together a sexy Patty Hearst costume.'
jokes.setup: The group rallies to rescue the Dean, described as alone and cold.
jokes.punchline: Britta's specific guess about the Dean's current activity — that he's making a sexy Patty Hearst costume — is a perfect character comedy moment: specific, weird, and probably accurate.
jokes.explanation: Best line in the episode. 'Sexy Patty Hearst costume' is an inspired detail — Patty Hearst is a historically specific, gender-role-challenging, slightly obscure reference that is exactly right for the Dean's costume aesthetic (he favors transgressive, provocative crossdressing). The specificity implies Britta knows him deeply enough to guess this accurately. 'Most likely' suggests resigned acceptance of the Dean's nature. It simultaneously delivers a great laugh AND is genuine character work for both Britta (knowing the Dean this well) and the Dean. Comparable to the best jokes in the reference corpus.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Britta's right.' / Britta: 'Wait, what?'
jokes.setup: Britta makes a correct observation and Jeff agrees.
jokes.punchline: Britta is so unaccustomed to Jeff agreeing with her that she can't process it — 'Wait, what?' — suggesting she's always wrong enough that this is a shock.
jokes.explanation: Classic running-gag beat — Britta is so routinely wrong that being right confuses everyone including herself. Great character economy. 'Wait, what?' in Britta's voice is the perfect two-word expression of imposter syndrome played as comedy.

jokes.text: Britta makes a correct, insightful point. Jeff: 'Britta's right.' / [beat] / 'Wait, what?'
jokes.setup: Britta correctly identifies the priority (rescuing the Dean over clearing their names).
jokes.punchline: Jeff's reflexive 'Britta's right' followed by his own shocked double-take — the idea of Britta being right is so unusual it startles him.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The 'Britta's right / wait, what?' beat is a well-established show joke that lands consistently because of the character dynamic. The double-take after is key. Character-dependent but effectively delivered.

jokes.text: 'We definitely never need to do another paintball.' / 'Yeah.' / 'See, therapy does work. We're cured.'
jokes.setup: The group resolves to rescue the Dean and return to Greendale.
jokes.punchline: The group reaches consensus that paintball should never happen again — a meta-resolution — and Jeff calls it therapeutic progress.
jokes.explanation: Callback to Abed's 'it feels forced' meta-commentary on paintball. The group unanimously agreeing to end paintball in a therapy-resolution context is a nice meta-bow. 'Therapy does work. We're cured.' is a funny deflation of the episode's therapy frame.

jokes.text: Chang villain meeting: 'Sounds like the study group has gotten wise to Operation Doppel-Deaner.'
jokes.setup: The villain reveal scene where Chang is monitoring the situation.
jokes.punchline: 'Operation Doppel-Deaner' — Chang has named his scheme to replace the Dean with a double using this portmanteau, which is both too clever and very stupid at the same time.
jokes.explanation: 'Doppel-Deaner' as an operation name is a very good bit — it shows Chang put effort into naming his scheme (the German prefix 'Doppel' for 'double' is correctly applied) while still being ridiculous. It's exactly the kind of thing an unhinged but not stupid person would name their plan. Chang-specific character comedy.

jokes.text: Chang: 'It's time for phase two.' / Henchman: 'What's phase two?' / Chang: 'Hey, I'm making up the same plan you are. Pitches, pitches, pitches.'
jokes.setup: Chang announces phase two of his plan in classic villain style.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't have a phase two — he admits to making it up in real time and calls for ideas ('Pitches, pitches, pitches'), completely undermining his villainous authority.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant subversion of the TV villain reveal. Chang sets up the cliché ('It's time for phase two') and then immediately admits he's winging it. 'Hey, I'm making up the same plan you are' — the frank admission that neither of them has a plan — combined with 'Pitches, pitches, pitches' (an improv workshop term) is a perfect character moment. Chang is chaotic, impulsive, and weirdly endearing. The energy of 'Pitches, pitches, pitches' is infectious. High quotability.

jokes.text: Henchman: 'Ah, thank you, Megan.' (to an unseen person bringing coffee or papers)
jokes.setup: Chang's villain lair apparently has office infrastructure including a staff member named Megan.
jokes.punchline: The henchman casually thanks 'Megan' — implying the criminal operation has mundane administrative support, an office worker in the middle of a villain's lair.
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist background joke — the mundane office-ness of the villain's operation (complete with a Megan doing support work) undercuts the drama. Brief but effective. The specificity of the name 'Megan' makes it funnier than 'thank you, assistant.'

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's late-night talk show: 'Troy and Abed in the Morning — Nights.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed's signature sign-on 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' plays as usual.
jokes.punchline: It's followed immediately by 'Nights.' — they're doing the morning show format at 3AM with a one-word format modification.
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of a beloved running gag. The 'Troy and Abed in the Morning' theme is iconic in the show, and 'Nights' as a simple suffix adaptation for their 3AM format is exactly the kind of minimal-effort absurd solution these two would arrive at. Very high character integration — this is entirely their world. The single-word adjustment is perfect in its economy.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Talk to us, lonely hearts. We got Jeff W. calling.' / Jeff (groggy): 'Who is this?' / Troy: 'Great question.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed's late-night show opens the phone lines and gets a call from Jeff.
jokes.punchline: Jeff, apparently woken up by a call from Troy and Abed, asks 'Who is this?' — and Troy responds 'Great question' as if fielding a profound inquiry rather than a confused person who doesn't know who called him.
jokes.explanation: Good bit. 'Great question' applied to 'Who is this?' is a funny talk-show host deflection — Troy treating Jeff's confused complaint as an interesting caller question. The late-night radio format applied to their friend group is well-executed.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed conducting a 3AM talk show, taking listener calls from a sleeping Jeff
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are running their late-night show and open the phone lines.
jokes.punchline: Their first caller is Jeff, who is apparently on their call list, waking him up at 3AM. Jeff: 'Who is this?' Troy: 'Great question.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the structure: they've called their sleeping friend as though he called in, and they treat his confusion ('who is this?') as a valid talk-show question ('Great question.'). It's both absurd and very true to Troy and Abed's relationship with their own bit.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed to sleepy Jeff: 'Stay on the line and we'll get your information. Yeah, we'll get you the help you need.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is annoyed at being called at 3AM and just wants to sleep.
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed treat Jeff's sleep complaint as a crisis requiring professional help — 'we'll get you the help you need' — turning his normal frustration into a mock crisis call.
jokes.explanation: Decent bit — the crisis-hotline framing for 'I want to sleep' is a mild but effective ironic reversal. Mostly works because of Troy and Abed's complete sincerity.

jokes.text: Annie calls in: 'Hey guys, long time, first time, love the show.' / Troy: 'Appreciate ya. How can we help?' / Annie: 'You can shut up and go to sleep.'
jokes.setup: Annie calls in using the proper radio call-in format: 'long time, first time, love the show.'
jokes.punchline: Despite the conventional radio-caller setup, her actual 'question' is just asking them to stop. She's played the format straight only to weaponize it.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in Annie's choice to participate in their format before destroying it. 'Long time, first time, love the show' establishes she knows the conventions — making 'you can shut up and go to sleep' funnier because she's used the structure against them. Very Annie: proper, structured, then exasperated.

jokes.text: Sign-off: 'may your dreams be sweet and your nightmares be "spooky monster" scary and not "grandma died" scary.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed sign off their late-night show.
jokes.punchline: Their sign-off blessing distinguishes between 'spooky monster' scary nightmares (acceptable) and 'grandma died' scary nightmares (not acceptable) — a taxonomy of nightmare severity delivered as a sincere wish.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The nightmare taxonomy ('spooky monster' vs. 'grandma died') is an inspired construction — it creates a whole emotional framework in six words. Everyone immediately understands the distinction because both types are real and distinct experiences. The sincerity of the wish makes it both funny and weirdly touching. Could only come from Troy (the childlike optimism, the specific emotional categories). Very high quotability and rewatch value. Approaches the 8.5+ tier.

tmdb_overview: After Abed is caught trespassing at Greendale, he and his friends visit a psychiatrist.
insight: Absurdist character comedy sustains an 81.5 score despite zero standout punchlines—pure consistency wins.
